analysis.one_liner: Taxes inheritances over $3.5 million at higher rates and closes trust loopholes used by the wealthiest families.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by a single senator with no cosponsors in September 2014, never got a committee hearing or vote, and died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would reinstate and raise the estate tax, which applies only to very large inheritances. Estates over $3.5 million would pay more, with a top rate of 55% on amounts over $50 million and a 10% surcharge on estates over $500 million. It would also close common loopholes: limits on valuing family businesses at artificial discounts, short-term trust tricks that dodge gift taxes, and gap between the value reported for estate tax and the value later claimed for income tax. Family farms would get a bigger break, with the farmland valuation exclusion rising from $750,000 to $3 million.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit indirectly, since the added revenue from very large estates reduces pressure on everyone else's taxes or supports public spending. Family farms and owners of conserved land get direct breaks: the farmland valuation exclusion rises to $3 million, and the estate tax exclusion for conservation easements rises to $2 million.

how_it_helps.text: Estates over $3.5 million face higher rates, with a 55% top rate on amounts over $50 million and a 10% surtax on estates over $500 million, and the basic exclusion drops from $5 million to $3.5 million [S2][S3].
The farmland valuation exclusion rises from $750,000 to $3 million and is adjusted for inflation, shielding working farms from estate tax pressure [S2][S3].
The estate tax exclusion for donated conservation easements rises to $2 million, and the excluded share of the easement's value rises from 40% to 60% [S2][S3].

The bill closes avoidance tools: it limits valuation discounts on family-owned business interests, requires 10-year minimum terms for grantor retained annuity trusts, and applies transfer taxes to grantor trusts [S2][S3].

Executors and donors must report the value of inherited or gifted property to the Treasury and to recipients, and heirs must use that same value for income-tax basis, closing the gap where estates were reported low for tax but high for later sale [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The heirs of the largest estates — those above $3.5 million — pay higher taxes, with the heaviest burden on the roughly 0.2% of estates over $50 million. Estate-planning professionals also lose business as the trust and valuation loopholes they sell are tightened.

drawbacks.text: Estate tax opponents argue it taxes wealth that was already taxed when earned, and that high rates can force heirs to sell family businesses or farms to pay the bill; the bill raises the top rate to 55% and lowers the exclusion to $3.5 million [S2][S3].

The bill adds new valuation and reporting rules — consistent basis reporting, limits on minority discounts, grantor trust rules — that increase compliance costs and complexity for executors, family businesses, and tax preparers, even those with modest estates [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct cost falls entirely on a small number of very large inheritances, and the bill deliberately softens the blow on farms and conserved land with larger exclusions. The main honest objection is the compliance burden and the long-running fairness debate over taxing inherited wealth twice; the bill's tightening of reporting rules is the part most likely to be felt by people who are not wealthy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never took it up, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Bernard Sanders (I-VT) introduced the bill in the Senate on September 18, 2014, less than four months before the Congress ended [S1][S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; no further action appears in the record [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill was never reported out of committee, debated, or voted on [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Heirs of the largest estates and the estate-planning industry, which keeps the valuation discounts and trust strategies the bill would have restricted. Nothing changed for anyone else.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Responsible Estate Tax Act on September 18, 2014.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over estate taxes; chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 18, 2014, and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; support was a single independent senator with zero cosponsors, and no senator of either party acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Very large estates and their heirs
industries.note: Estates over $3.5 million would pay higher rates, up to 55% above $50 million plus a surtax above $500 million. Because untaxed inheritances shift the tax burden onto other revenue sources, this industry's interest in keeping the bill off the floor ran against ordinary taxpayers' interest in who funds the government.

The bill restricts the valuation discounts, short-term GRATs, and grantor trust strategies that this profession sells to wealthy families to shrink their tax bills. Its business depends on the loopholes the bill closes.

Farms would become subject to the estate tax above the $3.5 million exclusion, but the special farmland valuation break rises from $750,000 to $3 million and adjusts for inflation, shielding most working farms from the bill's bite.

industries.industry: Land conservation organizations and land trusts
industries.note: Bigger estate tax exclusions for donated conservation easements — up to $2 million and 60% of value — give landowners a stronger incentive to conserve land, which land trusts administer.
